item.title: [simonwillison.net] Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
item.description:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

item.title: [simonwillison.net] GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
item.description:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

item.title: [simonwillison.net] GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
item.description:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights:

We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.

I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

item.title: [simonwillison.net] Ladybird's first alpha release
item.description:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925)  [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926)  [61 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72927)  [29 MB]
    ├── ProcessReaper (72928)  [1 MB]
    ├── Compositor (72930)  [123 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72953)  [36 MB]
    ├── WebContent (72984)  [819 MB]
    ├── MediaServer (73006)  [118 MB]
    ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007)  [20 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73052)  [144 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73057)  [73 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73073)  [166 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73094)  [70 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73112)  [116 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (73113)  [27 MB]
    └── WebContent (73185)  [60 MB]

Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

item.title: [andros.dev] Implementing Clean Architecture in Clojure
item.description:
Good architecture separates business logic from infrastructure. It is the foundation of almost every architecture you have studied. Separating responsibilities keeps you from being tied to a specific technology, like a database or a web framework, and as a side effect, it makes testing and modularity easier.

I decided to write this article because I needed to build a desktop application in Clojure, and the most natural option is Functional Core, Imperative Shell: the core of the application is only pure functions that receive data and return data. You will find it recommended in plenty of articles and talks because it fits so well with Clojure's immutability and pure functions. And if you use it, that's fine, it is very elegant to work with. However, it has a design problem that makes it hard to deal with uncertainty. If you don't know in advance what data you will need, the separation between the core and the infrastructure loses its clarity.

That is why I chose Clean Architecture, a first cousin of Hexagonal Architecture. It is a pattern I know in depth after applying it, and fighting with it, in other languages. Thanks to that experience, I was sure it would fit very well with a functional language.

This is not an article about Clean Architecture in general. If you are interested, I recommend reading my article Implementing Clean Architecture in Python. Broadly speaking, clean architecture splits the application into four layers:

flowchart TB
    subgraph EI["External Interfaces"]
        direction TB
        subgraph GW["Gateways"]
            direction TB
            subgraph UC["Use Cases"]
                direction TB
                E["Entities"]
            end
        end
    end
    style EI fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a8a
    style GW fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#14532d
    style UC fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d
    style E fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308,color:#713f12
  • Entities: The business data.
  • Use Cases: The business logic. They orchestrate the entities and talk to the outside world through interfaces.
  • Gateways: The interfaces the use cases need to interact with the outside world.
  • External Interfaces: The pieces that touch the real world, or infrastructure.
    • Database
    • File system
    • REST API
    • HTTP (website)
    • CLI

And one golden rule: inner layers cannot depend on outer layers. For example, use cases cannot import an external interface.

Therefore:

flowchart LR
    EI["External Interfaces"] -- "Calls come in through interfaces" --> CORE["Use Cases and Entities"]
    CORE -. "Results go out as simple structures" .-> EI
    style EI fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a8a
    style CORE fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d

The differences between Functional Core, Imperative Shell and Clean Architecture are not trivial.

Clean Architecture Functional core, imperative shell
Separation criterion Direction of dependencies Purity
Can the core do IO? Yes, through an interface Never
Dependency injection Protocols or functions Not needed
Core tests With test doubles Only input and output data
Data the core needs Asks for it when needed All of it upfront

Now, to adapt it to Clojure, we have to use the language's own quirks. Not much effort is needed, though, because Clojure's design already pushes you towards this pattern:

  • Data is immutable. An entity cannot change behind your back.
  • Maps are the universal structure. Maps go in, maps come out. No need to convert objects into DTOs, or DTOs into JSON.
  • Protocols are interfaces. They define a contract that any implementation can fulfil, without inheritance.
  • Functions are values. You can pass a dependency as an argument without any ceremony.

So each element of the architecture translates into its own nature:

  • Entities: Maps and functions. No classes, obviously.
  • Use Cases: Functions that orchestrate pure functions and side effects.
  • Gateways: Protocols.
  • External Interfaces: The libraries in the ecosystem that touch the real world: http-kit, Ring, Compojure, Hiccup, next.jdbc, etc.

Let's build a practical example and see how everything fits together.

Setting up the project

We are going to build a basic to-do list: create, list, mark as done and delete.

It will have two entry points in our infrastructure:

  • A REST API that returns JSON.
  • A web page with a few minimal forms, almost no HTML.

Both will use exactly the same use cases. That is the whole point of the architecture!

The folder structure will be the following:

  • tasks: The main project folder.
    • deps.edn: Dependencies and aliases.
    • src/tasks: Source code.
      • core: Business logic.
        • entities
          • task.clj
        • gateways
          • repository.clj
        • use_cases
          • response.clj
          • tasks.clj
      • infra: Infrastructure or external interfaces.
        • database
          • memory_repo.clj
        • api
          • routes.clj
        • http
          • routes.clj
      • main.clj

At first, our repository (database) will live in memory. Later we will iterate towards better solutions, such as a file on disk or a conventional database like SQLite.

About how namespaces work, in case you are not used to Clojure: dashes become underscores in folder names. For example, the namespace tasks.core.use-cases.tasks lives in src/tasks/core/use_cases/tasks.clj. Dependencies, on the other hand, are defined in deps.edn.

  • HTTP server: Ring + Jetty
  • Routing: Compojure
  • HTML rendering: Hiccup
  • JSON: data.json
  • Logs: slf4j-simple
;; deps.edn
{:paths ["src"]
 :deps {org.clojure/clojure {:mvn/version "1.12.7"}
        ring/ring-jetty-adapter {:mvn/version "1.15.6"}
        compojure/compojure {:mvn/version "1.7.2"}
        org.clojure/data.json {:mvn/version "2.5.2"}
        hiccup/hiccup {:mvn/version "2.0.0"}
        org.slf4j/slf4j-simple {:mvn/version "2.0.20"}}
 :aliases {:run {:main-opts ["-m" "tasks.main"]}}}

All the libraries will be used in the infrastructure, never in the core.

Now let's define the entities, the business data, as data and pure functions.

Entities

In other languages the entity would be a class. We will use a map.

{:id #uuid "b1ef0868-8e2b-4ce8-87cc-c3b55ed11e46"
 :title "Buy bread"
 :done? false}

Not only is it easy to read, it also converts to JSON effortlessly and it is safe, since there is no mutability.

Now we need pure functions that build, transform and validate tasks.

;; src/tasks/core/entities/task.clj
(ns tasks.core.entities.task
  (:require [clojure.string :as str]))

(def max-title-length 100)

(defn make-task
  "Build a new pending task."
  [id title]
  {:id id
   :title (str/trim title)
   :done? false})

(defn complete
  "Mark a task as done."
  [task]
  (assoc task :done? true))

(defn title-errors
  "Return the list of errors of a title. Empty if the title is valid."
  [title]
  (cond
    (not (string? title)) [{:field :title :message "Title is required"}]
    (str/blank? title) [{:field :title :message "Title can't be empty"}]
    (> (count (str/trim title)) max-title-length)
    [{:field :title :message (str "Title can't be longer than " max-title-length " characters")}]
    :else []))

The first reaction you would have in OOP is to make make-task generate a random id. Instead, we pass it in from outside. Generating a random identifier is a side effect, and we don't want side effects in the entities. The way it is designed now, the function always returns the same output for the same input. That is why it is a pure function.

Another detail is that complete does not modify the task. It returns a new one with :done? set to true, and the original stays intact.

Finally, title-errors does not throw exceptions. It returns a list of errors, empty if everything is fine.

We can try it in the REPL:

(complete (make-task 1 "  Buy bread  "))
;; {:id 1, :title "Buy bread", :done? true}

(title-errors "Buy bread")
;; []

(title-errors "   ")
;; [{:field :title, :message "Title can't be empty"}]

With the entities ready, let's write the use cases, which orchestrate the entities and call the infrastructure through interfaces. They are no longer pure functions: that is the price of being able to ask for data right when they need it.

Use cases

First, let's define the shape of the responses: a map with 3 keys that every use case will return.

;; src/tasks/core/use_cases/response.clj
(ns tasks.core.use-cases.response)

(defn success [data]
  {:type :success :errors [] :data data})

(defn parameters-error [errors]
  {:type :parameters-error :errors errors :data {}})

(defn resource-error [field message]
  {:type :resource-error :errors [{:field field :message message}] :data {}})

(defn system-error [error]
  {:type :system-error :errors [{:field :system :message (ex-message error)}] :data {}})
  • :success: Everything went fine.
  • :parameters-error: The input is wrong.
  • :resource-error: The process is correct, but the resource does not exist.
  • :system-error: Something blew up. An exception we have caught.

The use cases are the functions that implement the business logic: list, create, complete and delete tasks. They receive a repository as their first argument and return a response map.

;; src/tasks/core/use_cases/tasks.clj
(ns tasks.core.use-cases.tasks
  (:require [tasks.core.entities.task :as task]
            [tasks.core.gateways.repository :as repository]
            [tasks.core.use-cases.response :as response]))

(defn list-tasks [repo]
  (try
    (response/success {:tasks (repository/find-all repo)})
    (catch Exception error
      (response/system-error error))))

(defn create-task [repo title]
  (let [errors (task/title-errors title)]
    (if (seq errors)
      (response/parameters-error errors)
      (try
        (let [new-task (task/make-task (random-uuid) title)]
          (repository/save! repo new-task)
          (response/success {:task new-task}))
        (catch Exception error
          (response/system-error error))))))

(defn complete-task [repo id]
  (try
    (if-let [found (repository/find-by-id repo id)]
      (let [done (task/complete found)]
        (repository/save! repo done)
        (response/success {:task done}))
      (response/resource-error :id "Task not found"))
    (catch Exception error
      (response/system-error error))))

(defn delete-task [repo id]
  (try
    (if (repository/find-by-id repo id)
      (do (repository/delete! repo id)
          (response/success {:id id}))
      (response/resource-error :id "Task not found"))
    (catch Exception error
      (response/system-error error))))

As you can see, we never throw an exception. If something fails, we return an error map. Now it is predictable, and we can decide what to do with the error in the infrastructure.

This is dependency injection in Clojure: passing the dependency as an argument.

One nuance: random-uuid is still a side effect. We moved it out of the entity, we didn't remove it, and now it lives in the use case, which is allowed to have them. If a test needs a specific id, you can inject an id generator just like we inject the repository.

Now let's define the contracts the use cases need to interact with the infrastructure.

Gateways

The use cases call repository/find-all, repository/save!, etc. It may look like it, but we are not calling a database. We can't. Remember the rule: the core cannot depend on the infrastructure.

To solve the problem, we create a contract that states what the repository must do, and any concrete implementation can fulfil it.

In Clojure we use defprotocol to define a contract and defrecord to implement it.

First, we define the contract:

;; src/tasks/core/gateways/repository.clj
(ns tasks.core.gateways.repository)

(defprotocol TaskRepository
  (find-all [repo])
  (find-by-id [repo id])
  (save! [repo task])
  (delete! [repo id]))

Now let's implement the functions of the in-memory repository, which will store the tasks in an atom.

;; src/tasks/infra/database/memory_repo.clj
(ns tasks.infra.database.memory-repo
  (:require [tasks.core.gateways.repository :refer [TaskRepository]]))

(defrecord MemoryRepo [store]
  TaskRepository
  (find-all [_] (vec (vals @store)))
  (find-by-id [_ id] (get @store id))
  (save! [_ task] (swap! store assoc (:id task) task))
  (delete! [_ id] (swap! store dissoc id)))

(defn make-memory-repo []
  (->MemoryRepo (atom {})))

A detail: vals returns nil when the map is empty, and the API would reply null instead of an empty list. With vec we always return a vector.

An atom is a mutable reference to an immutable value. I don't want to overwhelm you with Clojure technicalities. Just keep in mind that it is the simplest way to manage state.

An example of how it works:

(def store (atom {}))

@store
;; {}

(swap! store assoc 1 "Buy bread")
;; {1 "Buy bread"}

(swap! store assoc 2 "Call mom")
;; {1 "Buy bread", 2 "Call mom"}

(swap! store dissoc 1)
;; {2 "Call mom"}

Now we can inject a MemoryRepo into the use cases.

It is time to build the infrastructure, the next layer.

Infra: REST API

The first entry point is a REST API. We will use Compojure for routing and data.json to read and write JSON: each route receives JSON, calls the use case and returns JSON.

All the code lives in src/tasks/infra/api/routes.clj, which starts by declaring its dependencies.

;; src/tasks/infra/api/routes.clj
(ns tasks.infra.api.routes
  (:require [clojure.data.json :as json]
            [compojure.core :refer [DELETE GET PATCH POST context]]
            [tasks.core.use-cases.tasks :as use-cases]))

First we need to translate the response type into an HTTP status code. A map is enough, and in Clojure a map can also be called as a function: (http-status :parameters-error) returns 400.

(def http-status
  {:success 200
   :parameters-error 400
   :resource-error 404
   :system-error 500})

This way we link each :type to its HTTP status code, so the infrastructure doesn't have to worry about business logic.

We also need a function that turns the use case result into an HTTP response with JSON.

(defn- json-response [result]
  {:status (http-status (:type result))
   :headers {"Content-Type" "application/json"}
   :body (json/write-str result)})

Another one to read the request body and parse it into a map.

(defn- read-body [request]
  (try
    (json/read-str (slurp (:body request)) :key-fn keyword)
    (catch Exception _ {})))

Finally, we define the API routes, which call the use cases and return the HTTP response.

(defn api-routes [repo]
  (context "/api/tasks" []
    (GET "/" []
      (json-response (use-cases/list-tasks repo)))
    (POST "/" request
      (json-response (use-cases/create-task repo (:title (read-body request)))))
    (PATCH "/:id" [id]
      (json-response (use-cases/complete-task repo (parse-uuid id))))
    (DELETE "/:id" [id]
      (json-response (use-cases/delete-task repo (parse-uuid id))))))

The API validates nothing, and it doesn't know what a valid title is: it only receives, translates and delivers. It is robust, because if the body is not valid JSON, read-body returns an empty map and the use case replies that the title is missing. It is also aligned with the architecture. The HTTP status codes are the ones that match each response type, and the body is JSON with the same map the use case returns.

The API infrastructure is done. Now let's go for the web.

Infra: HTML forms

The second entry point, or way to interact with the use cases, is a page with an HTML form. We will include a minimal interface to create, complete and delete tasks.

To render HTML we will use Hiccup, which represents HTML as vectors and maps.

For example, the following vector:

[:ul
 [:li "Buy bread"]
 [:li "Call mom"]]

Is equivalent to this HTML:

<ul>
  <li>Buy bread</li>
  <li>Call mom</li>
</ul>

We will use forms to create, complete and delete tasks. Each form sends a POST to the matching route and, if everything goes well, the server redirects to the home page.

;; src/tasks/infra/http/routes.clj
(ns tasks.infra.http.routes
  (:require [compojure.core :refer [GET POST routes]]
            [hiccup2.core :as h]
            [ring.util.response :refer [redirect]]
            [tasks.core.use-cases.tasks :as use-cases]))

(defn- task-item [{:keys [id title done?]}]
  [:li
   (if done? [:s title] title)
   (when-not done?
     [:form {:method "post" :action (str "/tasks/" id "/complete")}
      [:button "Done"]])
   [:form {:method "post" :action (str "/tasks/" id "/delete")}
    [:button "Delete"]]])

(defn- page [tasks errors]
  (str
   (h/html
    [:html
     [:body
      [:h1 "Tasks"]
      (for [{:keys [message]} errors]
        [:p message])
      [:form {:method "post" :action "/tasks"}
       [:input {:name "title"}]
       [:button "Add"]]
      [:ul (map task-item tasks)]]])))

(defn- html-response [status body]
  {:status status
   :headers {"Content-Type" "text/html; charset=utf-8"}
   :body body})

(defn http-routes [repo]
  (routes
   (GET "/" []
     (let [result (use-cases/list-tasks repo)]
       (html-response 200 (page (get-in result [:data :tasks]) (:errors result)))))
   (POST "/tasks" [title]
     (let [result (use-cases/create-task repo title)]
       (if (= :success (:type result))
         (redirect "/" :see-other)
         (html-response 400 (page (get-in (use-cases/list-tasks repo) [:data :tasks])
                                  (:errors result))))))
   (POST "/tasks/:id/complete" [id]
     (use-cases/complete-task repo (parse-uuid id))
     (redirect "/" :see-other))
   (POST "/tasks/:id/delete" [id]
     (use-cases/delete-task repo (parse-uuid id))
     (redirect "/" :see-other))))

Once again, the infrastructure knows nothing about the business logic. It translates the use cases into the language the browser speaks, and vice versa. To keep the example short, completing and deleting always redirect to the home page, without checking whether the use case returned an error.

Main

We are missing main.clj, the entry point where the application is assembled.

;; src/tasks/main.clj
(ns tasks.main
  (:require [compojure.core :refer [routes]]
            [ring.adapter.jetty :refer [run-jetty]]
            [ring.middleware.params :refer [wrap-params]]
            [tasks.infra.api.routes :refer [api-routes]]
            [tasks.infra.database.memory-repo :refer [make-memory-repo]]
            [tasks.infra.http.routes :refer [http-routes]]))

(defn -main []
  (let [repo (make-memory-repo)
        app (routes (api-routes repo)
                    (http-routes repo))]
    (run-jetty (wrap-params app) {:port 3000})))

Let's run it.

clojure -M:run

Let's try the API.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/tasks \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"title":"Buy bread"}'
{"type":"success","errors":[],"data":{"task":{"id":"ac089379-d761-4623-bce3-9f0fe6b7828f","title":"Buy bread","done?":false}}}

Now let's try to create a task with an empty title.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/tasks \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"title":""}'
{"type":"parameters-error","errors":[{"field":"title","message":"Title can't be empty"}],"data":{}}

Let's mark the task as done.

curl -X PATCH localhost:3000/api/tasks/ac089379-d761-4623-bce3-9f0fe6b7828f
{"type":"success","errors":[],"data":{"task":{"id":"ac089379-d761-4623-bce3-9f0fe6b7828f","title":"Buy bread","done?":true}}}

Now let's try the web version.

Open http://localhost:3000/ in the browser and you will see "Buy bread", crossed out. Add another task from the form and it will also show up in GET /api/tasks.

If we submit the form empty, the page shows the same error the API returned. The entity decided it, the web just displays it.

The full journey of a request:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant W as HTML form (infra)
    participant C as create-task (core)
    participant E as Task entity (core)
    participant R as MemoryRepo (infra)

    U->>W: POST /tasks title=Buy bread
    W->>C: (create-task repo "Buy bread")
    C->>E: (title-errors "Buy bread")
    E-->>C: []
    C->>E: (make-task uuid "Buy bread")
    E-->>C: {:id ... :title "Buy bread" :done? false}
    C->>R: (save! repo task)
    C-->>W: {:type :success ...}
    W-->>U: 303 redirect to /

Call arrows always point inwards. What comes back is always a map.

We've got it!

However, there is a small problem: if we restart the application, the tasks disappear. We need to store them somewhere more permanent, like the disk.

Infra: EDN repository

EDN (extensible data notation) is Clojure's native data format. It looks like JSON, but it supports more types: keywords, sets, UUIDs or dates. That is why our tasks are stored and read back as they are, #uuid included.

We only need another implementation of the same protocol.

;; src/tasks/infra/database/edn_repo.clj
(ns tasks.infra.database.edn-repo
  (:require [clojure.edn :as edn]
            [clojure.java.io :as io]
            [tasks.core.gateways.repository :refer [TaskRepository]]))

(defn- read-tasks [path]
  (if (.exists (io/file path))
    (edn/read-string (slurp path))
    {}))

(defn- write-tasks! [path tasks]
  (spit path (pr-str tasks)))

(defrecord EdnRepo [path]
  TaskRepository
  (find-all [_] (vec (vals (read-tasks path))))
  (find-by-id [_ id] (get (read-tasks path) id))
  (save! [_ task] (write-tasks! path (assoc (read-tasks path) (:id task) task)))
  (delete! [_ id] (write-tasks! path (dissoc (read-tasks path) id))))

(defn make-edn-repo [path]
  (->EdnRepo path))

And in main.clj we change a single line (plus its require).

;; src/tasks/main.clj
(ns tasks.main
  (:require ...
            [tasks.infra.database.edn-repo :refer [make-edn-repo]])) ; Changed

(defn -main []
  (let [repo (make-edn-repo "tasks.edn") ; Changed
        ...]))

Right in front of you is a practical example of how easy it is to change the infrastructure. Tomorrow it could be PostgreSQL or MongoDB, and the story would be the same: a new defrecord that fulfils TaskRepository.

However, reading and rewriting the whole file on every operation causes problems when several requests arrive at the same time: one write can overwrite another. We should use a conventional database like SQLite, which takes care of that.

Infra: SQLite repository

Unlike other languages, almost nobody uses an ORM in Clojure. It makes no sense to turn rows into objects when there are no objects. A row is already a map.

The ecosystem looks like this:

  • next.jdbc: The reference library. It includes functions like insert!, get-by-id or delete! for everyday CRUD.
  • HoneySQL: Write SQL as data structures.
  • HugSQL: Plain SQL in .sql files, turned into Clojure functions.
  • Toucan 2: The most complete option. It is the closest thing to an ORM, with models, hooks and column transformations.

We will use next.jdbc. We add next.jdbc and the SQLite JDBC driver to :deps in deps.edn.

;; deps.edn (in :deps)
com.github.seancorfield/next.jdbc {:mvn/version "1.4.72"}
org.xerial/sqlite-jdbc {:mvn/version "3.54.1.0"}

And a JVM option to the :run alias. The SQLite driver loads a native library, and recent Java versions warn about it on every start. This option silences the warning.

;; deps.edn (in :aliases)
:run {:jvm-opts ["--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED"]
      :main-opts ["-m" "tasks.main"]}

And the new repository.

;; src/tasks/infra/database/sqlite_repo.clj
(ns tasks.infra.database.sqlite-repo
  (:require [next.jdbc :as jdbc]
            [next.jdbc.result-set :as rs]
            [next.jdbc.sql :as sql]
            [tasks.core.gateways.repository :refer [TaskRepository]]))

(def ^:private options {:builder-fn rs/as-unqualified-maps})

(defn- row->task [{:keys [id title done]}]
  {:id (parse-uuid id)
   :title title
   :done? (= 1 done)})

(defn- task->row [{:keys [id title done?]}]
  {:id (str id)
   :title title
   :done (if done? 1 0)})

(defrecord SqliteRepo [datasource]
  TaskRepository
  (find-all [_]
    (map row->task (sql/query datasource ["SELECT * FROM tasks"] options)))
  (find-by-id [_ id]
    (some-> (sql/get-by-id datasource :tasks (str id) options) row->task))
  (save! [_ task]
    (let [{:keys [id title done]} (task->row task)]
      (jdbc/execute-one! datasource
                         ["INSERT INTO tasks (id, title, done) VALUES (?, ?, ?)
                           ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET title = excluded.title, done = excluded.done"
                          id title done])))
  (delete! [_ id]
    (sql/delete! datasource :tasks {:id (str id)})))

(defn make-sqlite-repo [path]
  (let [datasource (jdbc/get-datasource {:dbtype "sqlite" :dbname path})]
    (jdbc/execute! datasource ["CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks (
                                  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                                  title TEXT NOT NULL,
                                  done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"])
    (->SqliteRepo datasource)))

Look at the row->task and task->row functions. SQLite has no UUID or boolean types, and done? is not a valid column name in SQL without quotes. So the repository translates both: the UUID travels as text and :done? as a 0 or a 1. The rest of the details come straight from the next.jdbc documentation.

That said, SQLite guarantees that each write is atomic, but complete-task reads and then writes in two steps. In an application with heavy concurrency, you would wrap both in a transaction with jdbc/with-transaction.

To change the database, once again, we only change one line (plus its require).

;; src/tasks/main.clj
(ns tasks.main
  (:require ...
            [tasks.infra.database.sqlite-repo :refer [make-sqlite-repo]])) ; Changed

(defn -main []
  (let [repo (make-sqlite-repo "tasks.db") ; Changed
        ...]))

We run it, create a task from the form and another from the API, and look inside the database.

sqlite3 tasks.db 'SELECT * FROM tasks'
f2ef2060-0dd2-4627-928c-4302bf27a36d|Buy bread|0
fa7be8c4-ba42-4d4f-bcb7-02615d5acb36|Call mom|0

The infrastructure keeps changing, and the core stays intact.

Final notes

Back to the desktop application that brought me here: there, the infrastructure was the graphical interface, built with cljfx, and a JSON-RPC API. The core followed exactly the same structure. The infrastructure changes, not the business logic.

I have left testing out, it would deserve its own article. With this architecture it is extraordinarily cheap. The use cases are tested by injecting a MemoryRepo, and Ring routes are functions that receive a map and return another one, so they can be tested without starting the server.

One last thought about Functional Core. To get around the flaw I pointed out at the beginning, yogthos proposes modelling the flow as a state machine, where each step receives a map of resources as its first argument. More recently he took the idea further with a graph of components, where each node receives resources and state, and an orchestrator decides the next step. In my opinion, deep down it is the same idea as Clean Architecture: IO comes in as an explicit argument.

All the code is ready to run, tests included, in this repository.

I hope this article serves as a starting point for building Clojure applications with an architecture where the business logic is separated from the infrastructure.

Now it's time to open the REPL and paste the examples. There is no better teacher than practice.

item.description:
Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0

I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.

You can try it out in Datasette Lite here. It looks like this:

The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3, Observable Plot, and topojson-client), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.

Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.

As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.

The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account. Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.

The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.

I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.

Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

  • 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

item.title: [simonwillison.net] PostgreSQL 19 Released
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

item.title: [andros.dev] A Gopher server in 9 lines of Python
item.description:
There is no better way to learn a specification than implementing it.

Very recently I went from being an occasional Gopher reader to a writer. Little by little I understand the affection its community has for it, and the reasons why it is still alive beyond nostalgia.

Back to the matter at hand: I am one of those people who struggle to work with a technology they do not understand, even partially. So I started reading RFC 1436 (the Gopher specification). By browsing Gopherspace with Unix commands (nc, grep, sed, etc.), and checking the specification now and then, I learned how the protocol works and how it is implemented. That is why I decided to write a Gopher server in Python. Not to replace the existing software, which is mature and stable, but as one more exercise to dig deeper.

Fun fact: Python had its own Gopher library, gopherlib, which was removed in Python 2.6. You will not miss it much, though. A server fits in 9 lines of code.

import socket as Socket

socket = Socket.socket(Socket.AF_INET, Socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0)
socket.setsockopt(Socket.SOL_SOCKET, Socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
socket.bind(("0.0.0.0", 70))
socket.listen(5)
while True:
    connection, client_address = socket.accept()
    connection.send(str.encode("iHello world\t\tlocalhost\t70\r\n.\r\n"))
    connection.close()

If you run it and connect with a Gopher client to gopher://localhost, you will find a classic "Hello world". A heads-up: on Linux you will need sudo to open port 70, because it is a privileged port.

And that's it!

Let's go line by line. It is really interesting to see how Gopher works under the hood.

Minimal server

socket = Socket.socket(Socket.AF_INET, Socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0)
socket.setsockopt(Socket.SOL_SOCKET, Socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
socket.bind(("0.0.0.0", 70))
socket.listen(5)

The first lines are the TCP server: create the socket, listen, and wait for clients one at a time. Gopher is a text protocol that runs over TCP, so there is nothing else to do. Every request is a new connection, and the server remembers nothing about the previous one.

The RFC explicitly says the server keeps no state, which makes the implementation much simpler: no cookies, no sessions, no authentication, etc.

On top of that, it needs no encryption, so we can forget about TLS and certificates. And it listens on port 70, the one IANA assigned to Gopher, just like HTTP has port 80.

while True:
    connection, client_address = socket.accept()

The infinite loop serves the clients. accept() waits until someone connects and gives us connection, a socket to talk to that client. client_address is its IP and port: we do not use it in this server.

    connection.send(str.encode("iHello world\t\tlocalhost\t70\r\n.\r\n"))

Gopher has no headers and no status codes. Every response is either a menu or a text file.

In this case, we respond with a menu that has a single item: "Hello world". The line ends with \r\n, and the whole menu ends with a line containing only a period (.). So we are sending two lines: the item and the final period.

Every menu line has 5 parts:

Part In the example What it is for
Type i A character that says what the item is
Text Hello world What the user sees
Selector (empty) What the client will send if the item is clicked. Not used in this example
Host localhost The server where the item lives. It could be a different one if we want to point to another Gopher server
Port 70 Its port

The type, i in this case, sits right before the text. The other parts are separated by a tab (\t), and the line ends with \r\n.

Type i is an informational line: just text, no link. Fun fact: it does not appear in the RFC! It is an extension that almost every client accepts. The other types will show up in the next examples.

    connection.close()

Finally, we close the connection. According to the RFC, it is the server that closes it after responding. One request, one response, goodbye.

This is the sequence diagram of the interaction with the client:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server (port 70)
    C->>S: Opens a TCP connection
    C->>S: Selector + CRLF
    S->>C: Menu or file, ending with "."
    S->>C: Closes the connection

We now have the foundation of the server.

Gopher can return menus and text files. We already know how to return a menu. The second part is missing.

Serving menus and text files

A menu and a file are very different responses. A menu is made of lines with the 5 parts we just saw. A file is plain text, as is, ending with a line containing a period. No type, no tabs, no host.

But if there are no headers, how does the client know what it is going to receive? From the type of the link it clicked. If it clicked a type 1 item, it expects a menu. If it clicked a type 0 item, it expects a text file. The type lives in the link, not in the response.

And what does the client send when an item is clicked? That line's selector, as is, ending with \r\n. For the server it is an opaque string: it looks like a path, but it could be foo or 42. Each server interprets it however it wants. If it arrives empty, the client is asking for the main menu.

With these pieces we will build a small navigation. The main menu will have a type 1 item, "Documents", leading to another menu. This is the core of Gopher: menus linking to menus, like folders inside folders. Inside there will be a type 0 item, "About me", with the selector /docs/about.txt. When the user clicks it in their client, or requests it by hand with nc, the server will receive /docs/about.txt\r\n and respond with the file contents.

In short, the interaction flow will be:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: "" + CRLF
    S->>C: 1Documents TAB /docs TAB localhost TAB 70
    S->>C: Closes the connection
    Note over C: The user clicks "Documents"
    C->>S: /docs + CRLF
    S->>C: 0About me TAB /docs/about.txt TAB localhost TAB 70
    S->>C: Closes the connection
    Note over C: The user clicks "About me"
    C->>S: /docs/about.txt + CRLF
    S->>C: File contents + "."
    S->>C: Closes the connection

And if someone requests a selector that does not exist, we will respond with a type 3 item, the RFC's error type (the equivalent of an HTTP 40x or 50x).

On to the implementation.

We create about.txt next to the script:

Hi! I am Bob.
This text file is served over Gopher.

In the server, inside the infinite loop, we read the client's request and keep its first line: the selector. Depending on its value, we return a menu, a text file or an error.

data = connection.recv(1024).decode()
selector = data.split("\r\n")[0]

if selector in ("", "/"):
    # The main menu
    response = f"1Documents\t/docs\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

elif selector == "/docs":
    # A submenu
    response = f"0About me\t/docs/about.txt\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

elif selector == "/docs/about.txt":
    # Serve the file contents
    with open("about.txt") as file:
        response = file.read() + ".\r\n"

else:
    # Error
    response = f"3Not Found\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

connection.send(str.encode(response))

All together:

import socket as Socket

host = "localhost"
port = 70
socket = Socket.socket(Socket.AF_INET, Socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0)
socket.setsockopt(Socket.SOL_SOCKET, Socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
socket.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))
socket.listen(5)
while True:
    connection, client_address = socket.accept()
    data = connection.recv(1024).decode()
    selector = data.split("\r\n")[0]
    if selector in ("", "/"):
        response = f"1Documents\t/docs\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    elif selector == "/docs":
        response = f"0About me\t/docs/about.txt\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    elif selector == "/docs/about.txt":
        with open("about.txt") as file:
            response = file.read() + ".\r\n"
    else:
        response = f"3Not Found\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    connection.send(str.encode(response))
    connection.close()

We moved the host and port into variables so we do not repeat them.

Open gopher://localhost and you will see a single item, "Documents", which your client will show as a folder. Click it and you will enter a new menu with "About me", a text document. Click it and the file contents will appear, as is.

We have built a complete interaction flow, with menus and text files.

Now let's make our site a bit more interactive with type 7, the equivalent of an input.

Inputs and searches

Gopher has no forms or inputs, but it does have a type for searches: the RFC calls it Index-Search server. Although it was designed for search engines, nothing stops us from using it for anything else.

A type 7 item is written like any other menu line. When it is clicked, a client must ask the user for some text. Then it sends the selector, a tab, and whatever the user typed.

If we type "Cat" and the selector is /hello-user, the client will send:

/hello-user\tCat\r\n

According to the RFC, the response to a search is always a menu. And that is what we will do: we will ask for the user's name and return a menu with an informational line greeting them.

The interaction flow will be:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: "" + CRLF
    S->>C: 7Say hello TAB /hello-user TAB localhost TAB 70
    S->>C: Closes the connection
    Note over C: The user clicks "Say hello" and types "Cat"
    C->>S: /hello-user TAB Cat + CRLF
    S->>C: iHello Cat TAB TAB localhost TAB 70
    S->>C: Closes the connection

Back to the implementation.

Now the first line of the request can carry two parts separated by a tab. partition("\t") splits them: the selector on one side and the user's text on the other. If there is no tab, query is empty and everything works as before.

data = connection.recv(1024).decode()
selector, _, query = data.split("\r\n")[0].partition("\t")

if selector in ("", "/"):
    # The main menu, with a search item
    response = f"7Say hello\t/hello-user\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

elif selector == "/hello-user":
    # A menu with the greeting
    response = f"iHello {query}\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

else:
    # Error
    response = f"3Not Found\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"

connection.send(str.encode(response))

All together:

import socket as Socket

host = "localhost"
port = 70
socket = Socket.socket(Socket.AF_INET, Socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0)
socket.setsockopt(Socket.SOL_SOCKET, Socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
socket.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))
socket.listen(5)
while True:
    connection, client_address = socket.accept()
    data = connection.recv(1024).decode()
    selector, _, query = data.split("\r\n")[0].partition("\t")
    if selector in ("", "/"):
        response = f"7Say hello\t/hello-user\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    elif selector == "/hello-user":
        response = f"iHello {query}\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    else:
        response = f"3Not Found\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    connection.send(str.encode(response))
    connection.close()

Open gopher://localhost with your favorite client and you will see a single item, "Say hello", which your client will show as a search. Click it and it will ask you for some text. Type a name, for example "Cat", and confirm. The server will reply with a new menu: "Hello Cat".

Generating content on the fly

Our code writes every response at the moment it is requested, so nothing forces it to be fixed: we can generate content in real time. For example, listing the most voted stories on the Hacker News front page.

We will use the Algolia API, which returns the 10 front page stories with the most points in a single request. We will build one menu line for each.

Each story will be a type h item, a web link. Its selector starts with URL: followed by the address. Like i, it is not in the RFC: it is another extension that most clients understand.

Stories without an external link, such as "Ask HN" posts, will point to their discussion page.

import json
import socket as Socket
from urllib.request import urlopen

host = "localhost"
port = 70
api = "https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1"
socket = Socket.socket(Socket.AF_INET, Socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0)
socket.setsockopt(Socket.SOL_SOCKET, Socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
socket.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))
socket.listen(5)
while True:
    connection, client_address = socket.accept()
    data = connection.recv(1024).decode()
    selector = data.split("\r\n")[0]
    if selector in ("", "/"):
        response = f"iMost voted on the Hacker News front page\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n"
        with urlopen(f"{api}/search?tags=front_page&hitsPerPage=10") as page:
            stories = json.load(page)["hits"]
        for position, story in enumerate(stories, start=1):
            discussion = f"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id={story['objectID']}"
            url = story["url"] or discussion
            response += f"h{position}. {story['title']}\tURL:{url}\t{host}\t{port}\r\n"
        response += ".\r\n"
    else:
        response = f"3Not Found\t\t{host}\t{port}\r\n.\r\n"
    connection.send(str.encode(response))
    connection.close()

Open it and you will see a title followed by ten numbered links. Click any of them and your client will open the story in the browser. This is how it looked on November 18, 2026:

Most voted on the Hacker News front page
1. Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
2. Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
3. Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
4. Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales as revenues hit $104B
5. Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
6. ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in
7. Phrack 73
8. Microsoft's ONNX Runtime has disappeared from GitHub
9. MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash
10. 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed

The menu is generated on every request, so if you come back in a few hours you will see different stories.

This opens up endless possibilities: games, chats, interaction with LLMs, etc.

Conclusion

If you want to build a more serious Gopher server, some RFC details are missing, such as sending only ASCII text or doubling the periods at the start of a line. Since this is an academic exercise, it is not worth complicating it further.

All that is left for me to say is that I have learned a lot, and I hope you had fun too. Gopher is a simple protocol, but with a lot of potential. And while we are at it, it would not be a bad idea to start using it for your own projects.

See you in Gopherspace.
